details.description: In months where the patient denial rate ran at about 4%, companion denial rates in the same reporting ran at roughly 27-31%. The patient is permitted; the person who would carry her bag is not.
details.energy_note: Approved to go. Not approved to be helped.
details.notes: WHO monthly referral reports distinguish the two rates; the high figures sometimes quoted as patient denials are companion denials.

details.aspect: Which sends children to surgery with a stranger, or nobody
details.description: Where a parent is refused, the options are a grandparent who may also be refused, an unrelated approved adult, or the child travelling alone to a hospital in another jurisdiction.
details.energy_note: A seven-year-old, admitted alone.

details.aspect: For women it adds a social barrier to the administrative one
details.description: Travelling alone to another city for days of treatment is, for some families, not acceptable regardless of the permit. The refusal of a companion can therefore end the treatment entirely.
details.energy_note: Permitted by the army, forbidden at home.

details.aspect: The cost of going alone is counted nowhere
details.description: No interpreter of the family's situation, nobody to hear the discharge instructions, nobody to challenge a mistake, nobody to notice deterioration on the way back.
details.energy_note: Consented, medicated and discharged, with no witness.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the gap between the two rates
details.description: In months where patient denial ran at about 4%, companion denial in the same WHO reporting ran at roughly 27-31%. The patient is permitted to travel for treatment and the person who would accompany her is refused, at seven times the rate.
details.energy_note: She may go. Her mother may not.

issues.title: Which illness you have decides your odds at the window
issues.category_name: Health access, referrals and the medical permit
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living under the occupation, any gender
issues.summary: Approval rates vary substantially by medical specialty, which means the permit system performs a form of triage that no clinician designed and no patient is told about.

details.aspect: The spread
details.description: In January 2023: neurosurgery approvals ran at 90%, oncology 89% and cardiology 86%, while urology was 55%, internal medicine 68% and ophthalmology 72%.
details.energy_note: Your eyes are a lower priority than your heart, by policy.

details.aspect: Non-urgent is a category that becomes urgent
details.description: Conditions triaged as lower priority - eyes, urology, orthopaedics - deteriorate while they wait, and arrive later as the emergency they were not when first referred.
details.energy_note: Waiting until it qualifies as serious.

details.aspect: Women's conditions cluster in the lower-priority specialties
details.description: Gynaecological, urological and chronic pain conditions are precisely the categories least likely to be treated as urgent by a permit system, and the ones most likely to be under-reported by the patient in the first place.
details.energy_note: A system that ranks what women mostly present with, low.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - January 2023, by specialty
details.description: Neurosurgery approvals ran at 90%, oncology 89% and cardiology 86%, while urology was 55%, internal medicine 68% and ophthalmology 72%. The same permit office, the same month, a thirty-five point spread depending on the diagnosis.
details.energy_note: Your odds at the window depend on which organ.

issues.title: Evacuation as the only remaining option
issues.category_name: Health access, referrals and the medical permit
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living under the occupation, any gender
issues.summary: Where the health system is destroyed rather than merely restricted, treatment means leaving the territory entirely - a process with a small quota, a closed crossing and no return guarantee.

details.aspect: The numbers, and where they stop
details.description: WHO recorded 7,841 patients permitted medical evacuation and referral from Gaza between October 2023 and 29 September 2025, with about two thirds - 5,000, or 63.8% - evacuated before Israeli forces took the Rafah crossing on 7 May 2024.
details.energy_note: The route closed, and the number stopped.

details.aspect: Evacuation separates the patient from the family
details.description: Approval is for the patient, sometimes one companion. A mother evacuated for treatment leaves her other children behind in a place she cannot easily return to.
details.energy_note: Treated abroad, and unable to get back.

details.aspect: There is often no route home
details.description: Once outside, re-entry depends on a crossing that may not reopen. Medical evacuation can become permanent displacement without anyone deciding that it should.
details.energy_note: Left for six weeks of treatment. Never came back.

details.aspect: Research now describes the referral system itself as a weapon
details.description: Peer-reviewed work published in 2026 addresses 'the weaponization of medical referrals and evacuations' during the war - treating the permit process as an instrument rather than a bureaucracy.
details.energy_note: The referral form, reclassified as ordnance.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the day the route closed
details.description: WHO recorded 7,841 patients permitted medical evacuation from Gaza between October 2023 and 29 September 2025 - about two thirds of them, 5,000, before Israeli forces took the Rafah crossing on 7 May 2024. One date accounts for the shape of the entire series.
details.energy_note: Two thirds before one Tuesday, a third after.

issues.title: Giving birth at a checkpoint
issues.category_name: Women: the body, birth, guardianship and personal status law
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Palestinian identity and being female
issues.summary: The most documented single intersection of occupation and gender. Labour does not wait for a gate to open, and the road between a village and a maternity ward has soldiers on it.

details.aspect: The headline figures
details.description: Palestinian Ministry of Health figures record at least 68 pregnant women giving birth at Israeli checkpoints since 2000, with 35 miscarriages and the deaths of five women. A Lancet analysis found 10% of pregnant Palestinian women were delayed at checkpoints each year from 2000 to 2007 on the way to give birth.
details.energy_note: Sixty-eight women, delivered on a road.
details.notes: HONEST CAVEAT: most versions of this figure trace to a single originating source, the Palestinian MoH, relayed by UN agencies and journals. Small discrepancies appear between versions (68 vs 69; 2006 vs 2007; miscarriages vs infant deaths). The data also concentrates on 2000-2007 and is not current.

details.aspect: The year-by-year breakdown
details.description: UN reporting: 2000-2001, 31 women delivered at checkpoints and 17 babies died; 2002, 16 women and 11 babies; 2003, 8 women and 3 babies; 2004, 6 women and 5 babies.
details.energy_note: A number that is also a list of specific nights.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - ambulances held, in a five-month sample
details.description: The Palestinian Red Crescent documented 10 deliveries in ambulances between January and May 2005 at the El-Toufah checkpoint in Gaza alone, all within delays of one and a half to two hours.
details.energy_note: Ten births in ambulances, at one checkpoint, in five months.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - Houria Miri, 2002
details.description: Prevented for several hours from reaching an ambulance, she collapsed from severe haemorrhage. After an emergency caesarean her baby died and she remained critical for days.
details.energy_note: A named woman, and several hours.

details.aspect: The adaptation is to give birth at home
details.description: The Ministry of Health registered a 7.9% increase in home deliveries in the West Bank. Women choose the known risk of an unattended birth over the unknown risk of the road.
details.energy_note: Choosing the kitchen floor over the checkpoint.

details.aspect: Or to move house weeks in advance
details.description: Women in villages behind closures relocate to a relative's home near the hospital for the last weeks of pregnancy - abandoning their household, work and other children to be on the correct side of a gate.
details.energy_note: Moving out of your own home to be allowed to give birth.

details.aspect: The legal framing exists and has gone nowhere
details.description: UNFPA has argued that a birth at a checkpoint, or an inability to refer a woman in labour because of a military barrier, breaches human and reproductive rights; the Lancet work considered it against the Rome Statute's criteria for crimes against humanity. Despite UN resolutions since April 2005, no legal recourse has been taken.
details.energy_note: Twenty years of resolutions, no case.

details.aspect: Inadequate pregnancy care is a leading cause of death for women here
details.description: Inadequate medical care during pregnancy has been described as the third leading cause of death among Palestinian women of childbearing age. The checkpoint is one input into that, and the input nobody can plan around.
details.energy_note: Third on the list, and entirely administrative.

issues.title: Two authorities, one journey: the guardian rule on top of the permit
issues.category_name: Women: the body, birth, guardianship and personal status law
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Palestinian identity and being female
issues.summary: A Palestinian woman in Gaza needs Israel's permission to leave and, since 2021, may be stopped by a male relative's application to a court. Either alone would be a hurdle; together they are a trap with two keys and she holds neither.

details.aspect: The February 2021 notice
details.description: Gaza's Supreme Judicial Council issued a notice on 14 February 2021 allowing male guardians to restrict unmarried women's travel. It came five days after Egypt exceptionally opened the border indefinitely - i.e. precisely when leaving had become possible.
details.energy_note: The door opened, and a second lock appeared.

details.aspect: The original version, and the amendment
details.description: The first version required unaccompanied women to obtain permission from a male guardian - a husband, a relative, or even a son. After a backlash led by rights groups it was amended: instead, a male relative may petition a court to stop her travelling if it would cause 'absolute harm'.
details.energy_note: Amended from 'ask your son' to 'your brother may sue'.

details.aspect: The procedural trap inside the amendment
details.description: HRW notes she can be prevented from travelling as soon as the guardian applies - before any court has ruled. The application itself is the block. Women cannot prevent men from travelling.
details.energy_note: Stopped by the filing, not by the verdict.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - Afaf al-Najar, 19
details.description: She won a scholarship to study communications in Turkey, secured every travel document, and paid $500 to skip the long lines at Rafah. Palestinian border officials blocked her in September 2021. She appealed to local rights groups, who appeared reluctant to help for fear of reprisal, and eventually filed a petition herself.
details.energy_note: A scholarship, all the paperwork, $500, and a relative's signature.

details.aspect: The company it puts Gaza in
details.description: HRW's 2023 'Trapped' report lists the jurisdictions where male guardians can ban women's travel abroad as Iran, Gaza, Saudi Arabia and Yemen, with Qatar permitting court-imposed bans on female relatives.
details.energy_note: On a list of four.

details.aspect: Two vetoes means planning is irrational
details.description: Applying for a scholarship, a job or a conference requires assuming both approvals. Many women stop applying, which is invisible to both authorities and appears in no statistic either of them keeps.
details.energy_note: Two people can say no, so you stop asking.

details.aspect: And it removes the standard escape route
details.description: For women elsewhere, leaving is the exit from a controlling family. Here the family can block the exit through a court, and the occupation can block it through a permit, so the option that exists everywhere else does not exist.
details.energy_note: Nowhere to go, twice over.

issues.title: Personal status law: two territories, two codes, neither written here
issues.category_name: Women: the body, birth, guardianship and personal status law
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Palestinian identity and being female
issues.summary: Family law in the West Bank is Jordanian, in Gaza it is Egyptian, and both predate the Palestinian Authority. A woman's rights in marriage, divorce, custody and inheritance depend on which occupation-era statute her postcode inherited.

details.aspect: The two codes
details.description: For Muslims, the Jordanian Personal Status Law No. 61 of 1976 applies in the West Bank and the Egyptian Law of Family Rights of 1954 in Gaza. The wider landscape mixes Palestinian, Ottoman and British Mandate law with Israeli military orders.
details.energy_note: Your marriage is governed by a 1954 Egyptian statute.
details.source_name: UNFPA/UN Women, Gender Justice & The Law

details.aspect: Inheritance at half, and often not even that
details.description: Sharia inheritance rules give a daughter half a son's share. Enforcement is a separate problem: in practice in Gaza women often do not receive even that, and may be pressured or threatened by male relatives not to file a claim at all.
details.money_note: Value of the share not received.
details.energy_note: Half by law, and nothing by arrangement.

details.aspect: Guardianship sits with the father regardless
details.description: Fathers are the sole legal guardians of children. A mother with custody may still be unable to enrol, treat, or travel with her own child without the father's signature.
details.energy_note: Custody of a child you cannot sign for.

details.aspect: Divorce is asymmetric by construction
details.description: Men may divorce by repudiation without going to court. Women have access only to limited types of divorce, obtainable through a court, on grounds they must prove.
details.energy_note: He says a sentence. You bring a case.

details.aspect: It contradicts the Basic Law and nothing follows from that
details.description: Analysts note these sex-specific rights and duties are not consistent with the equality guarantee in Article 9 of the Amended Basic Law. The contradiction has been identified for two decades without resolution.
details.energy_note: Unconstitutional, and still the law.

details.aspect: Fragmentation is itself the obstacle to reform
details.description: Because the law differs between the West Bank and Gaza, and the two administrations are divided, any unified reform requires a political reconciliation that has not happened. Women's rights are hostage to a separate dispute.
details.energy_note: Reform blocked by an argument that is not about you.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - two codes, neither written by Palestinians
details.description: Family law for Muslims is the Jordanian Personal Status Law No. 61 of 1976 in the West Bank and the Egyptian Law of Family Rights of 1954 in Gaza. A woman's rights in marriage, divorce, custody and inheritance depend on which foreign statute her territory inherited from a previous occupier.
details.energy_note: Governed by Cairo, 1954, or Amman, 1976.

issues.title: The killing that gets a reduced sentence
issues.category_name: Women: the body, birth, guardianship and personal status law
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Palestinian identity and being female
issues.summary: The provision granting a pardoning excuse for so-called honour killings was annulled in 2011. The articles that reduce the sentence anyway were not, and the courts continue to use them.

details.aspect: What Article 340 did
details.description: Under the Jordanian penal code of 1960 applicable in the West Bank, a man who surprised his wife or a female relative committing adultery and killed or harmed her was entitled to a 'pardoning excuse'. Only men could benefit; a woman in the same circumstances could not invoke it.
details.energy_note: An excuse in the statute book, for killing her.

details.aspect: It was repealed, and the sentences still fall
details.description: A 2011 presidential decree annulled Article 340 in the West Bank and amended Article 18 of the 1936 Mandate code in Gaza. But Articles 97, 98 and 99 still permit reduced punishments, and in Gaza courts often give reduced sentences on honour grounds despite no legal basis for doing so.
details.energy_note: The excuse was deleted. The discount remained.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the Nablus sentence, four times over
details.description: A first instance court used articles 97 and 98 to reduce the sentence to two and a half years. On appeal he was convicted of premeditated murder and sentenced to 25 years. Article 99 and time served cut that to 10. The cassation court then reduced the charge again.
details.energy_note: Twenty-five years, then ten, then less.

details.aspect: The label is used to hide other motives
details.description: Women Media and Development (TAM) reported that killings actually motivated by inheritance or revenge were framed as honour crimes so the killer would receive a lighter sentence. The discount creates an incentive to claim it.
details.energy_note: Call it honour and the sentence halves.

details.aspect: The count
details.description: WCLAC documented 23 killings of Palestinian women and girls in 2016 across the Palestinian territory, many claimed to be honour-based.
details.energy_note: Twenty-three, in one year, in a small population.

details.aspect: One reform did land
details.description: The 'marry-your-rapist' provision, which extinguished prosecution if the perpetrator married the victim, was repealed in 2018.
details.energy_note: One clause, genuinely gone.

details.aspect: Impunity is social before it is legal
details.description: Lawyers working on these cases argue the impunity is not encoded simply in the letter of the law - the culture has historically been more tolerant when the killing is justified by honour, and that is what the judges are drawn from.
details.energy_note: The statute is only half of it.

details.aspect: What it means day to day for a woman who is not in danger
details.description: The existence of a reduced-sentence route changes the calculation behind every argument about where she goes, who she speaks to, and what she wears - not because anyone threatens her, but because the discount is known to exist.
details.energy_note: A background pressure that never has to be stated.

issues.title: Managing a period when there is nothing to manage it with
issues.category_name: Women: the body, birth, guardianship and personal status law
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Palestinian identity and being female
issues.summary: Under siege and displacement, menstruation becomes a logistics problem with no supplies, no privacy, no water and no disposal - and the coping strategy that emerged is pharmacological.

details.aspect: The supply situation
details.description: The siege prevented menstrual pads and tampons entering alongside fresh water, soap and toilet paper. Women have torn edges off shelter tents and pieces of clothing to use as pads.
details.energy_note: Cutting up the tent you are sleeping in.

details.aspect: Norethisterone as the workaround
details.description: Women turned to norethisterone, normally prescribed for painful or heavy periods, to suppress menstruation entirely. Side effects include irregular bleeding, nausea, cycle changes, dizziness and mood swings. Local sources report even the pills have become scarce.
details.money_note: Per course, where obtainable at all.
details.energy_note: Switching your body off because there is no alternative.

details.aspect: The stated reason is dignity, not convenience
details.description: A Gaza City psychologist described more women turning to the pills to avoid the embarrassment and shame caused by the lack of hygiene, privacy and health products - not to avoid the period itself.
details.energy_note: Medicated against humiliation.

details.aspect: The health consequences of the alternative
details.description: Unsanitary materials and prolonged product use cause urinary tract infections, bacterial vaginosis, menorrhagia and abnormal discharge - conditions that then need the health system that is not there.
details.energy_note: An infection caused by the lack of a pad.

details.aspect: It is a recognised rights question, and recognition changes nothing yet
details.description: Analysts invoke CEDAW's provision on adequate living conditions in relation to water and sanitation; the UN Special Rapporteur on water and sanitation has described water being used as a weapon of war in Gaza.
details.energy_note: Named at the UN, unresolved on the ground.

details.aspect: This one does not appear in war reporting at all
details.description: Of everything in this dataset it is among the most universal - it affects roughly half the displaced population every month - and among the least written about, because it is the part people will not describe afterwards.
details.energy_note: Half the population, monthly, and almost no coverage.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - what the tents are being cut up for
details.description: With menstrual products, water and soap prevented from entering, women have torn the edges off shelter tents and pieces of clothing to use as pads - and turned to norethisterone to suppress menstruation entirely, with local sources reporting that even the pills have become scarce.
details.energy_note: Cutting up the tent you sleep in, because there is nothing else.

issues.title: Being pregnant while it is happening
issues.category_name: Women: the body, birth, guardianship and personal status law
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Palestinian identity and being female
issues.summary: Pregnancy does not pause for a war. Where the health system has collapsed, the ordinary complications become fatal and the ordinary procedures are performed without anaesthesia.

details.aspect: Caesareans without anaesthesia
details.description: Health providers reported surgical procedures including caesarean sections conducted without anaesthesia and at times without electricity. Aid workers described women undergoing caesareans and emergency operations without sterilisation, anaesthesia or painkillers.
details.energy_note: Abdominal surgery, awake.

details.aspect: Discharged three hours later
details.description: Many mothers are discharged as little as three hours after giving birth because bed numbers collapsed with the hospitals. One account describes a woman discharged after a caesarean without pain medicine, recovering from major surgery in a tent with a newborn.
details.energy_note: Major surgery, then a tent, the same afternoon.

details.aspect: The miscarriage rate
details.description: Health authorities report the miscarriage rate rising to nearly 50%, an increase of more than 70% on pre-war averages. In one month the Gaza Health Ministry recorded about 920 miscarriages among roughly 2,000 pregnancies - about 460 per 1,000, against a pre-war average of 140 per 1,000. Nearly 4,000 miscarriages in six months.
details.energy_note: One pregnancy in two.

details.aspect: The clinical picture behind it
details.description: A UN report found about 74% of pregnancy losses occurred in the first trimester and 57% of pregnant women were anaemic. Close to half of all births were by caesarean, nearly all for bleeding, hypertension and infection.
details.energy_note: Anaemic, hypertensive, infected, and pregnant.

details.aspect: Most receive no prenatal care at all
details.description: Most pregnant women in Gaza never receive a prenatal checkup, leaving conditions such as preeclampsia undiagnosed - a driver of postpartum haemorrhage, the leading cause of maternal death.
details.energy_note: The thing that kills you, undetected because nobody looked.

details.aspect: It did not stop with the ceasefire
details.description: Doctors report the pattern continuing after the ceasefire that took effect in October 2025, because the causes are displacement, destroyed homes, collapsed primary care and living in tents without running water - none of which a ceasefire repairs.
details.energy_note: The shooting stopped and the miscarriages did not.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - one month, 920 miscarriages in 2,000 pregnancies
details.description: The Gaza Health Ministry recorded about 920 miscarriages among roughly 2,000 pregnancies in a single month - about 460 per 1,000, against a pre-war average of 140 per 1,000. A UN report found about 74% of losses occurred in the first trimester and 57% of pregnant women were anaemic.
details.energy_note: Four hundred and sixty losses per thousand pregnancies.

issues.title: Early marriage, and the reasons that are not tradition
issues.category_name: Women: the body, birth, guardianship and personal status law
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Palestinian identity and being female
issues.summary: Marriage ages are set at 18 in the West Bank and 17 in Gaza and can be lowered by a judge with a guardian's approval. Where movement, education and income are all constrained, marriage becomes the available route and the constraint is read afterwards as culture.

details.aspect: The legal ages and the exception
details.description: 18 in the West Bank under the Jordanian law and 17 in Gaza, though ages can be lowered where a judge allows it with the guardian's approval. Under Gaza's Law of Family Rights the law assumes a guardian exists, and where none does the qadi acts as one.
details.energy_note: A minimum age with a judge-shaped hole in it.

details.aspect: Economic pressure is the actual driver
details.description: Where a daughter cannot reach a university, cannot get a permit to work, and the household has lost its income, marriage transfers the cost of her maintenance. Families describe it in exactly those terms.
details.energy_note: Married off by an economy, not a tradition.

details.aspect: It forecloses the education that would have been the exit
details.description: Leaving school at 17 to marry ends the qualification track, which ends the independent income, which makes divorce unaffordable, which is a different constraint for the next forty years.
details.money_note: Lifetime earnings difference.
details.energy_note: One year's decision, forty years of consequence.

details.aspect: Qualitative work finds the reflections are long and mixed
details.description: A 2026 study of West Bank women's long-term reflections on early marriage finds neither a uniform tragedy nor a benign norm - which is why this row is marked secondary and probabilistic rather than stated as a harm.
details.energy_note: Not one story. A distribution.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the judicial exception
details.description: Marriage ages are 18 in the West Bank and 17 in Gaza, but can be lowered where a judge allows it with a guardian's approval. Under Gaza's Law of Family Rights the law assumes a guardian exists, and where none does, the qadi acts as guardian - so the consent required can be supplied by the court itself.
details.energy_note: The minimum age, waivable by the man who applies it.

issues.title: The family unification freeze
issues.category_name: Family separation, reunification and split households
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Palestinian identity, ID, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Since 2002 Israelis and Jerusalem residents have been barred from obtaining status for a Palestinian spouse from the occupied territory. The measure was temporary in 2002 and is still in force.

details.aspect: The sequence
details.description: In May 2002 Israel froze all processing of family unification applications with Palestinian spouses from the occupied territory. In August 2003 the moratorium was enshrined in law as a temporary order, on security grounds.
details.energy_note: A temporary order, twenty-three years old.

details.aspect: The asymmetry is the design
details.description: Israelis who marry foreigners who are not residents of the occupied territory may apply as before and the spouse can obtain status. The bar applies only to the one population.
details.energy_note: Marry anyone in the world. Except from there.

details.aspect: The outcomes for those inside the process
details.description: Between January 2000 and July 2013, 43% of family unification applications were rejected - 20% on security grounds, 13% for lack of proof of centre of life. Of 12,284 applications, 5,629 were approved and 4,249 rejected.
details.energy_note: Four in ten marriages, refused by a ministry.

details.aspect: Those who got through live on annual permits
details.description: The few who entered the process after the 2002 freeze live on temporary stay permits only - no stability, no social security rights, no health rights, and annual security vetting.
details.energy_note: Married, resident, and re-vetted every year.

details.aspect: Gaza was banned outright in 2008
details.description: Israel completely banned family unification with individuals from Gaza in 2008. For those couples there is no process to be refused by.
details.energy_note: Not refused. Not possible.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - fifteen years of Thursdays
details.description: She has a blue Jerusalem ID, he has a green West Bank one. They married in 2009. He has never been permitted to live in the flat. He comes when a permit allows, which is not most weeks, and their daughter has worked out that asking when he is coming makes her mother go quiet.
details.energy_note: A marriage conducted in visits.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the outcomes, 2000 to 2013
details.description: Of 12,284 family unification applications between January 2000 and July 2013, 5,629 were approved and 4,249 rejected - a 43% rejection rate, 20% on security grounds and 13% for lack of proof of centre of life. Israel banned unification with individuals from Gaza outright in 2008.
details.energy_note: Four thousand two hundred and forty-nine marriages, refused.

issues.title: Living together illegally in your own country
issues.category_name: Family separation, reunification and split households
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Palestinian identity, ID, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Where the registry will not align two spouses' addresses, the family lives together in breach of the rules, in constant exposure to detention and forcible transfer.

details.aspect: Thousands of families are in this position
details.description: Israel's refusal to change addresses, combined with forcible transfers back to Gaza, leaves couples with non-matching registered addresses living together in the West Bank in constant fear.
details.energy_note: At home, and liable to be removed from it.

details.aspect: The exposure is total and permanent
details.description: Harassment, detention, deportation, forcible transfer to Gaza, or a re-entry ban - and the risk applies at every checkpoint, every ID check and every hospital admission, for as long as the family exists.
details.energy_note: Every routine document check is the one that could end it.

details.aspect: It constrains everything downstream
details.description: The policy restricts the rights to work, to study and to seek medical care, because each of those requires presenting an ID that will show the mismatch.
details.energy_note: Can't work, study or be treated without showing them.

details.aspect: Women disproportionately bear it
details.description: Because marriage typically moves the woman to the husband's area, it is overwhelmingly women who end up resident under the wrong registered address - which is why Gisha found most victims of the transfer procedure are women.
details.energy_note: The one who moved is the one who is illegal.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the procedure built to refuse
details.description: A Freedom of Information response revealed that the 'Procedure for handling applications by Gaza Strip residents for settlement in the Judea and Samaria Area', in place since 2009, is designed for rejecting applications rather than accepting them. Gisha titled its report 'A procedure so special it applies to no one'.
details.energy_note: A form whose function is the refusal.

issues.title: Visiting someone in prison
issues.category_name: Family separation, reunification and split households
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Palestinian identity and being female
issues.summary: Prison visits require a permit, a route through several checkpoints, an entire day, and frequently end in refusal at the last gate. The person doing this is almost always a woman.

details.aspect: The visit is a full-day operation
details.description: Coach at dawn, several checkpoints, a search, a wait, then a short visit through glass, then the return. A visit measured in minutes costs a day, every time.
details.money_note: Transport and fees, per visit.
details.energy_note: Fourteen hours for forty-five minutes.

details.aspect: The permit can fail at any point in the chain
details.description: Approved in advance, refused at the gate, on grounds not given. The day is spent either way and so is the money.
details.energy_note: Turned back at the last door, with no reason.

details.aspect: Children's visits are separately restricted
details.description: Children over a certain age are frequently barred, so a parent must choose which child comes, or explain to a child why they are the one who cannot.
details.energy_note: Choosing which of your children sees their father.

details.aspect: The role is gendered and unpaid
details.description: The mothers, wives, sisters and daughters run the visits, the lawyer contact, the canteen money and the appeals, on top of the household they are now the sole manager of.
details.time_note: Days per year on visits and prisoner administration.
details.energy_note: An unpaid second job with no end date.

issues.title: The family spread across four jurisdictions
issues.category_name: Family separation, reunification and split households
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Palestinian identity, ID, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: An ordinary extended family may hold West Bank, Gaza, Jerusalem, Israeli and diaspora documents. No single event - a wedding, a funeral, an anniversary - can lawfully be attended by all of them.

details.aspect: There is no venue that works
details.description: Choose the West Bank and the Gaza relatives cannot come. Choose Amman and the green IDs need permits. Choose Europe and almost nobody gets a visa. The gathering cannot be held anywhere on earth.
details.energy_note: No country on the planet where the family can all stand.

details.aspect: So the funerals are the losses that compound
details.description: Deaths do not schedule. The relatives who cannot come do not come, and the absence is permanent in a way a missed wedding is not.
details.energy_note: Burying people in front of a phone screen.

details.aspect: Grandparents and grandchildren who have never met
details.description: Where the documents never align, a generation grows up knowing relatives only as voices. This is the commonest and least remarked-upon outcome of the whole regime.
details.energy_note: A grandmother known entirely as a phone call.

details.aspect: The family stops functioning as an economic unit
details.description: Extended families elsewhere pool childcare, housing, capital and care for the old. Fragmentation across permit regimes removes that, so each household carries alone what would have been shared.
details.energy_note: All the costs a family normally splits, paid singly.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the choice put to a woman at a crossing
details.description: Gisha documented the bind under the title 'Give up your right to live in the West Bank, or never see your children in Gaza again'. One woman was told at a crossing either to return to the West Bank as her ID address required, or to sign a form changing her address to Gaza - forcing a choice between her family home in Nablus and her son in Gaza.
details.energy_note: A house or a child, decided at a window.

issues.title: The university as a target
issues.category_name: Education, universities and credentials
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living under the occupation, any gender
issues.summary: Palestinian universities are raided, their students detained in numbers, and UN experts describe this as systematic policy rather than episodic violence.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - Birzeit, 6 January 2026
details.description: Israeli soldiers and military vehicles stormed the campus with more than 8,000 students present, smashing the main gate and firing across campus. Over forty people, mostly students, were injured. Sources said the raid followed a student solidarity event for Palestinian prisoners.
details.energy_note: Eight thousand students, and grenades on the lawn.

details.aspect: The UN's characterisation and the numbers
details.description: UN experts said the assault on Birzeit is 'not episodic violence but a systematic policy', reporting 463 university students detained - 148 of them from Birzeit - plus 27 higher education staff, most under administrative detention. 'The purpose is disruption.'
details.energy_note: Four hundred and sixty-three students, in custody.

details.aspect: Female students are specifically targeted
details.description: The Palestinian Prisoner's Society described the arrest of four female Birzeit students in overnight raids across Ramallah as reflecting a longstanding policy targeting university students, particularly women.
details.energy_note: Arrested at 3am for being a student.

details.aspect: Families are not told the charges
details.description: It is common for families and institutions to receive little information regarding the charges, so a household loses a daughter to a system that does not explain what she is accused of.
details.energy_note: Gone, and nobody will say what for.

details.aspect: The degree takes longer, and that costs money
details.description: Raids, closures, detentions and rescheduled exams extend a three-year degree by semesters. Each added semester is fees, rent, and a year of earnings not started.
details.energy_note: A degree that keeps getting longer.

issues.title: Winning the scholarship and not being able to take it
issues.category_name: Education, universities and credentials
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Palestinian identity, ID, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Admission is the easy part. The visa, the exit permit, the guardian's consent and the crossing all have to align, and each is separately capable of ending it.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the Irish refusal rate, and the collapse in it
details.description: Irish Department of Justice figures show 103 Palestinian long-stay study visa refusals against 39 issued up to 21 August - a 27.5% approval rate, down from 83.8% the previous year.
details.energy_note: An approval rate that fell by two thirds in a year.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - appeal by post, from a place with no post
details.description: There is no internationally recognised postal service in Gaza, yet Irish authorities require appeals to be submitted by post with original documents. The appeal route exists and cannot be used.
details.energy_note: Appeal by post. There is no post.
details.notes: A pure example of a procedure that is formally open and practically void.

details.aspect: The scale of the blockage
details.description: As of February 2024, more than 555 students in Gaza were unable to travel abroad for admissions and scholarships already granted to them.
details.energy_note: Five hundred and fifty-five places, unused.

details.aspect: Deferral is not usually available
details.description: Funding bodies and universities defer for a year at most, and often not at all. A blocked departure is a forfeited place, not a postponed one.
details.money_note: Value of a forfeited funded place.
details.energy_note: The scholarship does not wait.

details.aspect: For women it is one more permission on the stack
details.description: Admission, funding, visa, exit permit, crossing - and, in Gaza since 2021, no male relative petitioning to stop it. Five approvals, any one of which is fatal.
details.energy_note: Five separate yeses, and one no ends it.
details.notes: See WOM-002 and BOR-003 for the Afaf al-Najar case, which failed at the last two of these simultaneously.

issues.title: A qualification from a place the world is unsure about
issues.category_name: Education, universities and credentials
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Palestinian identity, ID, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Credential recognition assumes a stable issuing authority, an archive that can be written to, and a postal route. Where those are damaged, a real degree becomes unprovable.

details.aspect: Verification requires an institution that still exists
details.description: Credential evaluators write to the issuing university for confirmation. Where the university has been destroyed or its records lost, there is no one to answer, and an unanswered verification is treated as a failed one.
details.energy_note: Your degree is real and unconfirmable.

details.aspect: Curricula do not map cleanly
details.description: West Bank and Jordanian universities have tried to give displaced students final-exam access to complete degrees, but differences between curricula complicate transfer, so partial study frequently converts into nothing.
details.energy_note: Three years of study that count for nothing anywhere.

details.aspect: Requalification costs the productive decade
details.description: Re-sitting professional examinations abroad in a second language, while working, takes years that arrive exactly when a career would otherwise be compounding.
details.energy_note: Starting again at thirty-four.

details.aspect: Which pushes qualified people into unqualified work
details.description: The pharmacist drives, the engineer delivers, the teacher cleans - for the years the recognition takes, and often permanently, because the years themselves close the door.
details.money_note: Lifetime earnings difference from downgraded work.
details.energy_note: Qualified, and driving.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the Irish appeal that cannot be posted
details.description: Irish authorities require study-visa appeals to be submitted by post with original documents. There is no internationally recognised postal service in Gaza. The appeal route formally exists and cannot be used by the people it applies to.
details.energy_note: Appeal by post, from a place with no post.

issues.title: A work permit tied to one employer
issues.category_name: Work, permits, brokers and wage theft
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living under the occupation, any gender
issues.summary: The permit is issued in an Israeli employer's name after an army security clearance. It binds the worker to that employer, that area and a curfew, which is the structural cause of everything in WRK-002.

details.aspect: How it is issued
details.description: Permits are issued only when an Israeli employer files a request with the interior ministry, and only after the worker passes an army security clearance. The permit is written in the employer's name.
details.energy_note: Your right to work belongs to your boss.

details.aspect: And what it restricts
details.description: Workers may travel only to their designated work area and must return to the West Bank before a set hour or risk arrest. The permit is a movement licence with a curfew attached.
details.energy_note: A job with a legal bedtime.

details.aspect: Complaining costs the permit
details.description: Because the permit is in the employer's name, raising unpaid wages, unsafe conditions or an injury risks the employer withdrawing the request - which removes the permit, the income and the ability to enter at all.
details.energy_note: Every labour right, conditional on not using it.

details.aspect: Security clearance is unexplained and inheritable in practice
details.description: A refusal is given without reasons, cannot be argued, and frequently attaches to a family rather than an individual.
details.energy_note: Unemployable because of a file you can't read.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - 100,000 permits withdrawn at once
details.description: Some 100,000 Palestinians had work permits revoked after October 2023, leaving them confined to the West Bank where jobs are scarce and wages far lower. Israel maintains it has no obligation to permit entry for work and decides on security considerations.
details.energy_note: A hundred thousand livelihoods, ended in a week.

issues.title: The broker who sells you your own permit
issues.category_name: Work, permits, brokers and wage theft
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living under the occupation, any gender
issues.summary: A permit bound to one employer and issued in scarce quantities produces a black market. It is large, measured by Israel's own central bank, and the worker pays for it out of the wage the permit lets him earn.

details.aspect: The size of the market
details.description: Roughly 30% of work permits have been delivered in exchange for a brokerage fee of NIS 1,500-2,500. The Bank of Israel put broker profits at NIS 122 million in 2018. That year, 45% of the 94,254 Palestinian workers in Israel got their jobs through agents, who could take up to a third of a worker's wages.
details.money_note: NIS 1,500-2,500 per permit, often monthly.
details.energy_note: A third of the wage, to be allowed to earn it.

details.aspect: What it costs the individual
details.description: Workers reported paying around NIS 2,500 - about USD 688 - for documents obtained through dishonest means, often nearly half their total income, paid out of pocket. Kav LaOved documented monthly fees of NIS 1,500-3,500 per worker.
details.money_note: Per month, recurring.
details.energy_note: Half your pay, to the man who sold you the paper.

details.aspect: Who actually profits
details.description: One middleman alone issued permits for 200 workers at NIS 2,000-3,000 each per month, and was one link in a chain; most of the money reportedly ended up with former Israeli security personnel closer to those issuing permits. Contractors hold quotas they do not need and resell permits for around NIS 2,000 after paying NIS 1,400.
details.energy_note: A quota, bought at 1,400 and sold at 2,000.

details.aspect: The reform did not end it
details.description: A new system adopted in 2020 was meant to end the black market and did not end the role of agents. The ITUC has called for ILO fair recruitment standards under which recruitment fees are not borne by workers.
details.energy_note: Reformed, and still for sale.

details.aspect: Post-2023 the price tripled
details.description: Some 100,000 Palestinians had permits revoked after October 2023. A former Tulkarem job-placement operator says Palestinian brokers now charge more than triple the pre-war price.
details.money_note: Post-2023 broker price, per permit.
details.energy_note: Scarcer permits, triple the price.

details.aspect: The whole arrangement is invisible in the wage statistics
details.description: Recorded earnings look like a wage. The worker's actual take-home is that minus a third, and no dataset of Palestinian incomes subtracts it.
details.energy_note: Every income figure for this group is overstated.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - one middleman, two hundred workers
details.description: A single middleman issued permits for 200 workers at NIS 2,000-3,000 each per month, and was one link in a chain - most of the money reportedly ending up with former Israeli security personnel closer to those issuing permits. Contractors hold quotas they do not need and resell permits for around NIS 2,000 after paying NIS 1,400.
details.energy_note: Bought at fourteen hundred, sold at two thousand, monthly.

issues.title: Wage theft that cannot be reported
issues.category_name: Work, permits, brokers and wage theft
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living under the occupation, any gender
issues.summary: Where the intermediary collects the wage, the worker often does not know who the employer legally is - which makes every labour protection unusable.

details.aspect: You may not know who employs you
details.description: Workers relying on intermediaries often do not know their actual Israeli employer. The intermediary collects wages directly and deducts fees before passing on the remainder.
details.energy_note: Can't sue them. Don't know their name.

details.aspect: Off the books means no rights accrue
details.description: Kav LaOved documents workers paid off the books, denying them social rights, sick pay and holidays, plus unlawful dismissals. Years of work produce no pension entitlement and no injury cover.
details.money_note: Unaccrued social rights over a working life.
details.energy_note: Thirty years of work, no pension record.

details.aspect: An injury ends the income permanently
details.description: An undocumented worker injured on an Israeli site has no accident cover, cannot easily prove the employment relationship, and loses the permit along with the ability to work.
details.energy_note: Hurt at work, and instantly unemployed and uninsured.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the Bank of Israel's own estimate
details.description: The Bank of Israel put broker profits at NIS 122 million in 2018, the year in which 45% of the 94,254 Palestinian workers in Israel obtained their jobs through agents who could take up to a third of a worker's wages. The central bank of the state operating the permit system measured the market the system created.
details.energy_note: A hundred and twenty-two million shekels, measured by the central bank.

issues.title: Women's work, and why the participation rate is what it is
issues.category_name: Work, permits, brokers and wage theft
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Palestinian identity and being female
issues.summary: Female labour force participation is very low, and the usual explanation is culture. The mechanical explanations - checkpoints, childcare, permit exclusion and safety - come first.

details.aspect: The commute is the first filter
details.description: A job requiring a checkpoint crossing is a job with an unpredictable arrival time and an evening risk. Households that would accept a woman working locally will not accept that, and employers will not accept the lateness.
details.energy_note: Ruled out by the road, before anyone mentions culture.

details.aspect: The permit economy is almost entirely male
details.description: Work permits for Israel are overwhelmingly issued for construction and agriculture. The largest single source of Palestinian wage income is structurally closed to women.
details.energy_note: The one big employer doesn't hire women.

details.aspect: Childcare does not exist as a market
details.description: Where incomes are low and extended families are scattered by the permit regime, the childcare that would release a woman into work is neither affordable nor available.
details.energy_note: No nursery, no grandmother nearby, no job.

details.aspect: So the qualified stay home
details.description: Palestinian women's educational attainment is high relative to their participation rate. The gap between what they are trained for and what they do is the specific waste this row records.
details.money_note: Lifetime earnings foregone.
details.energy_note: Educated for a job the geography won't allow.

details.aspect: And the outcome is attributed to their culture
details.description: The low participation rate is read abroad, and sometimes at home, as evidence about Palestinian attitudes to women working - which relocates the responsibility from the checkpoint to the family.
details.energy_note: Blamed for a statistic the roads produced.
details.notes: See PSY-002.

issues.title: PayPal serves the settlement and not the village
issues.category_name: Banking, payments and digital financial exclusion
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Palestinian identity, ID, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: The clearest single example of digital exclusion drawn along national lines rather than geographic ones: the same territory, two populations, one of which has payment services.

details.aspect: The disparity, stated plainly
details.description: PayPal operates in Israel including in settlements in the occupied West Bank, but does not grant Palestinians with West Bank and Gaza bank accounts access to its platform. Over five million Palestinians are excluded. Settlers, banks and merchants in the settlements use it freely on Israeli accounts.
details.energy_note: Same hillside. One side can get paid.

details.aspect: The stated reason, and the problem with it
details.description: PayPal cites a 'high risk' environment. It also operates in Somalia and Yemen. Palestinian-American businessman Sam Bahour notes Palestine has a functioning banking sector, all Palestinian banks have correspondent US banks making daily transfers, and the US Treasury has praised Palestinian banking compliance. Visa, Mastercard and Apple Pay operate there.
details.energy_note: Too risky for here, fine for Somalia.

details.aspect: Congress and shareholders have raised it and nothing changed
details.description: Eleven members of Congress wrote to the CEO before the May 2023 shareholder meeting. Harrington Investments, which pushed divestment from apartheid South Africa, filed a shareholder motion for a non-discrimination policy. The campaign has run since 2016.
details.energy_note: A decade of letters.

details.aspect: The legal characterisation
details.description: Advocates argue the policy appears based on national or ethnic origin rather than location, which would breach the prohibition on discrimination in international human rights law.
details.energy_note: A geography rule that tracks an ethnicity exactly.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the comparison that undoes the risk argument
details.description: PayPal cites a 'high risk' environment for not serving Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. It operates in Somalia and Yemen. Visa, Mastercard and Apple Pay operate in the Palestinian territories, and the US Treasury has publicly praised Palestinian banking compliance.
details.energy_note: Too risky for Ramallah, acceptable in Mogadishu.

issues.title: Freelancing with no way to be paid
issues.category_name: Banking, payments and digital financial exclusion
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Palestinian identity, ID, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Remote work is the obvious answer to a closed border. The payment layer is where it fails, and the failure is expensive rather than absolute.

details.aspect: The payout rails are closed
details.description: PayPal and Payoneer both exclude Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank while Israeli settlers in the same territory retain access. Most freelancing platforms rely on payout methods Palestinians cannot fully use.
details.energy_note: Hired, delivered, and unable to collect.

details.aspect: The workaround has a 20-30% tax on it
details.description: On Upwork, Palestinian freelancers often lose another 20-30% of earnings to currency-exchange intermediaries - on top of the platform's own fee.
details.money_note: Annual loss to intermediaries at typical freelance income.
details.energy_note: A quarter of every invoice, gone to the plumbing.

details.aspect: And the accounts that do work are precarious
details.description: A freelancer at Gaza Sky Geeks described accounts being closed and funds frozen with no access until much later, and said the account is only usable for small inconsistent transfers - otherwise it risks closure.
details.energy_note: Keep the payments small so they don't notice you.

details.aspect: The remaining routes are worse
details.description: Western Union, a relative's account, cryptocurrency, or registering a company abroad. Each is expensive, insecure, or available only to a narrow slice of people.
details.energy_note: Four bad options and no good one.

details.aspect: Which caps the size of anything anyone builds
details.description: A business cannot scale past the payment method. The ceiling is not talent, market or capital; it is that nobody can invoice properly.
details.energy_note: A company that can never get bigger than a bank transfer.

issues.title: Compliance as a permanent surcharge
issues.category_name: Banking, payments and digital financial exclusion
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Palestinian identity, ID, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: For Palestinians abroad, financial life is not blocked so much as taxed - additional checks, delays, refused products and worse rates, indefinitely.

details.aspect: The friction tax
details.description: Transfers reviewed, payments queried, new accounts turned into multi-week processes with extra documents. Individually minor, cumulatively a permanent surcharge on ordinary financial life.
details.money_note: Annual, in fees, spreads and delay.
details.energy_note: A percentage off the top of your whole life.

details.aspect: Credit builds slower or not at all
details.description: Restricted products and refused cards mean a thinner file, which means a worse mortgage a decade later - a six-figure difference produced by an origin field.
details.energy_note: A worse mortgage for a worse birthplace.

details.aspect: And there is nothing to appeal
details.description: A closure or refusal letter gives no reason, because giving one may constitute tipping off. There is no accusation to rebut and every subsequent institution sees the closed account.
details.energy_note: Declined, permanently, with no charge stated.
details.notes: Structurally identical to FIN-001 in assets/text/iran.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - fifteen thousand accounts at one bank
details.description: A 2024 FinCEN comment from the National Iranian American Council documented Bank of America identifying as many as 15,000 accounts connected to individuals of Iranian heritage that had been restricted, and described the problem as systemic across the sector. The same de-risking logic is applied to Palestinian-origin customers, which is why this row sits in both datasets.
details.energy_note: Fifteen thousand accounts, one bank, one heritage.
details.notes: Cross-reference: recorded in full in assets/text/iran.

issues.title: An economy with somebody else's currency and customs
issues.category_name: Banking, payments and digital financial exclusion
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living under the occupation, any gender
issues.summary: The Palestinian economy uses the shekel, and its import duties and VAT are collected by Israel and remitted - or withheld - as a political instrument.

details.aspect: No monetary policy, because no currency
details.description: The Palestine Monetary Authority is not a central bank in the usual sense. There is no rate to set, no currency to devalue, and inflation is imported wholesale from another economy.
details.energy_note: An economy with no steering wheel.

details.aspect: Clearance revenues are collected by the other side
details.description: Import duties and VAT on goods entering for the Palestinian market are collected by Israel and transferred to the PA - and periodically withheld, at which point public salaries are paid at a fraction.
details.money_note: Household effect of a partial salary month.
details.energy_note: Your salary depends on a political decision elsewhere.

details.aspect: Partial salaries land on households, mostly on women
details.description: When public sector pay arrives at 60% or 70%, the household budget is rebuilt by whoever runs it - cutting food, deferring medicine, borrowing from family - which is generally the woman.
details.energy_note: Told in the morning that this month is sixty per cent.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the salary month that arrives at sixty per cent
details.description: Import duties and VAT on goods entering for the Palestinian market are collected by Israel and transferred to the PA - and periodically withheld, at which point public sector salaries are paid at a fraction. The household budget is then rebuilt by whoever runs it.
details.energy_note: Told on payday that this month is partial.

issues.title: Held on 2G by spectrum allocation
issues.category_name: Telecom, spectrum and being held on 2G
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living under the occupation, any gender
issues.summary: Israel controls frequency allocation under the Oslo framework. Palestinian operators got a sliver of spectrum in 1999 and kept it while their subscriber base multiplied twentyfold.

details.aspect: The allocation, frozen
details.description: Israel licensed Jawwal just 4.8 MHz in the 900 MHz band in 1999. Jawwal retained that same allocation while its subscriber base grew from 120,000 to more than 2.5 million, limited to a 2G system with mobile internet over EDGE.
details.energy_note: Twenty times the users, the same sliver of air.

details.aspect: 3G arrived twelve years late, and not everywhere
details.description: Israel launched 3G in 2004 and blocked Palestinian access to the frequencies for nearly twelve years. In November 2015 it agreed to allow 3G in the West Bank only; it launched in January 2018. Israel had already granted 4G licences to six Israeli operators in 2015. Gaza has only ever had 2G.
details.energy_note: A generation of technology, withheld for twelve years.

details.aspect: The second operator never reached Gaza at all
details.description: Wataniya won a combined 2G/3G licence in 2006 with a $354 million bid, received it in March 2007, and could not launch commercially in the West Bank until November 2009. It was never able to begin operations in Gaza because of restrictions on spectrum and imports, leaving Gaza a monopoly market.
details.energy_note: Paid $354 million for a licence it couldn't use.

details.aspect: The measured economic cost
details.description: The World Bank found the Palestinian mobile sector lost over $1 billion in potential earnings across three years, largely from Israeli restrictions, with over 20% of West Bank customers using Israeli providers for speed.
details.energy_note: A billion dollars, in three years, in a small economy.

details.aspect: Slow networks exclude people from the modern economy
details.description: Remote work, online study, telemedicine, e-government and digital payments all assume bandwidth. A 2G household is excluded from each of them regardless of the person's skills.
details.energy_note: Qualified for the remote job, and unable to join the call.

details.aspect: And the network you do have routes through the other side
details.description: Both operators license spectrum from the Israeli government, route traffic through Israel, and must use an Israeli-registered company for international links. EFF noted that with Palestinian telcos locked to less secure 2G, interception is easier even for users of Palestinian carriers.
details.energy_note: Your call is carried by the people you're hiding from.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - a $354 million licence that could not be used
details.description: Wataniya Mobile Palestine won a combined 2G/3G licence in 2006 with a $354 million bid and received it in March 2007, but could not launch commercially in the West Bank until November 2009 - and was never able to begin operations in Gaza at all, because of Israeli restrictions on spectrum access and on importing equipment.
details.energy_note: Three hundred and fifty-four million dollars, for a network in one half of a territory.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - 4.8 MHz, held flat for nineteen years
details.description: Israel licensed Jawwal 4.8 MHz in the 900 MHz band in 1999. The allocation did not change while the subscriber base grew from 120,000 to more than 2.5 million - a twentyfold increase in users on an unchanged sliver of spectrum.
details.energy_note: Twenty times the users, the same air.

issues.title: The blackout as an instrument
issues.category_name: Telecom, spectrum and being held on 2G
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living under the occupation, any gender
issues.summary: Connectivity can be cut, and when it is, it removes the ability to call an ambulance, reach family, verify a rumour or document anything.

details.aspect: What goes with the signal
details.description: Emergency calls, family contact, banking, aid registration, news and any ability to record what is happening. It is not an inconvenience layer; it is the layer everything else runs on.
details.energy_note: No ambulance, no mother, no proof.

details.aspect: It falls hardest on those least mobile
details.description: A person who can walk to find signal does. An elderly woman, a woman in late pregnancy, a mother with four children under eight, cannot.
details.energy_note: Signal exists two kilometres away, which may as well be Mars.

details.aspect: Not knowing is its own injury
details.description: Uncertainty about whether a specific person is alive produces a stress response that does not habituate, because there is no information to adapt to.
details.energy_note: The one state the mind cannot settle into.
details.notes: Parallel to INF-001 in assets/text/war.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - Gaza has only ever had 2G
details.description: Wataniya was never able to begin operations in Gaza because of Israeli restrictions on spectrum and imports, leaving it a single-operator market that has only ever run 2G. When Israel agreed in November 2015 to permit 3G, the agreement covered the West Bank only.
details.energy_note: Two generations of mobile technology, never delivered at all.

issues.title: Being surveilled as the default condition
issues.category_name: Telecom, spectrum and being held on 2G
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living under the occupation, any gender
issues.summary: Phone, movement, social media and facial recognition data are collected at a density that changes what people are willing to say and where they are willing to go.

details.aspect: Assume the phone is read
details.description: The reasonable operating assumption is that calls, messages and location are available to the authorities. Whether or not any particular message is read, the assumption does the work.
details.energy_note: Self-censoring in your own text messages.

details.aspect: A social media post is a permit risk
details.description: Posts have grounds consequences: permit refusals, detention, and - abroad - visa and naturalisation consequences. The cost of an opinion is quantifiable and high.
details.energy_note: A post that could cost a hospital appointment.

details.aspect: Which removes the ordinary outlet for what is happening
details.description: The normal human response to a bad year is to describe it to people. That is precisely the behaviour that carries risk here, so the processing does not happen.
details.energy_note: Nowhere safe to say any of it.
details.notes: See PSY-003.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - why the network generation matters for surveillance
details.description: The Electronic Frontier Foundation noted that with Palestinian telecoms locked to less secure 2G, Israel may have interception access even to users of Palestinian carriers - and that both operators must route traffic through Israel and use an Israeli-registered company for international links.
details.energy_note: The old network is the readable one.

issues.title: Water that is not drinkable
issues.category_name: Siege: water, power, fishing limits and the dual-use list
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living under the occupation, any gender
issues.summary: Gaza's only natural water source has been over-pumped and contaminated to the point where almost none of it is fit to drink, and the fixes require imports that the closure restricts.

details.aspect: The proportion
details.description: 96.2% of household water from the coastal aquifer is non-potable. Earlier assessments put it at 90-95% unfit due to nitrogen and chloride; the World Bank reported only 5-10% of the aquifer yields drinkable water.
details.energy_note: Ninety-six per cent of the tap water, undrinkable.

details.aspect: The mechanism
details.description: The aquifer was being over-abstracted by 100 million cubic metres a year - almost double the safe rate - because desalination plants were not built, causing falling groundwater and seawater intrusion.
details.energy_note: Pumped at twice the rate it refills.

details.aspect: So drinking water is a purchased commodity
details.description: Households buy from private tankers and vendors of uncertain quality - a recurring cash cost, in one of the poorest places, for something that comes out of a tap elsewhere.
details.money_note: Annual household spend on drinking water.
details.energy_note: Paying cash, weekly, for water.

details.aspect: Only a quarter of households had daily running water even before
details.description: Only a quarter of households received running water every day, and then for several hours only. The rest live on a rota and store what they can.
details.energy_note: Water arrives on a timetable, if at all.

details.aspect: Which makes the household water manager's day
details.description: Filling, storing, rationing, boiling, allocating between drinking, cooking, washing and laundry - a daily logistics job that falls almost entirely on women and is counted as leisure in every time-use survey.
details.time_note: Cumulative days per year on water logistics.
details.energy_note: Two hours a day, on water, uncounted.

details.aspect: And 90 million litres of sewage went into the sea daily
details.description: Untreated and partially treated sewage discharged off the coast at that rate creates a public health hazard that returns through the groundwater and the fish.
details.energy_note: It goes into the sea and comes back in the water.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the pumping arithmetic
details.description: The coastal aquifer was being over-abstracted by 100 million cubic metres a year, almost double the safe rate, because desalination plants were not built. 96.2% of household water from it is non-potable, and the World Bank reported only 5-10% of the aquifer yields drinkable water.
details.energy_note: Pumped at twice the safe rate, until it turned to seawater.

issues.title: Electricity by the hour
issues.category_name: Siege: water, power, fishing limits and the dual-use list
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living under the occupation, any gender
issues.summary: A chronic deficit means power arrives in blocks and everything - study, refrigeration, medical equipment, water pumping - is scheduled around it.

details.aspect: The baseline
details.description: Outages of up to 12 hours a day. With additional fuel and purchased Israeli electricity, supply ran 10-15 hours a day depending on demand after October 2018, against 5-7 hours before it.
details.energy_note: Five hours of power a day, in living memory.

details.aspect: It cascades into the water supply
details.description: Pumping, treatment and desalination all need power, so an electricity deficit is also a water deficit and a sanitation deficit. OCHA linked increased electricity supply directly to improved water access.
details.energy_note: No power, therefore no water, therefore no sanitation.

details.aspect: Household life is rebuilt around the schedule
details.description: Laundry, baking, charging, homework and pumping all happen in the window. Missing the window means the task waits a day, and the person doing the waiting is whoever runs the house.
details.energy_note: Doing the washing at 2am because that's when it's on.

details.aspect: Refrigeration failure is a food and medicine cost
details.description: Insulin, vaccines and food all need a cold chain. Intermittent power means spoilage that is paid for repeatedly by households with no margin.
details.energy_note: Throwing away food you couldn't afford, again.

details.aspect: And it ends the possibility of most kinds of work
details.description: No manufacturing, no reliable remote work, no data centre, no cold storage business. The power schedule sets a ceiling on what industries can exist.
details.energy_note: Whole industries, ruled out by a generator.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - five to seven hours a day
details.description: Before October 2018 Gaza had 5-7 hours of electricity a day; additional fuel for the power plant and purchased Israeli electricity raised it to 10-15 hours depending on demand, against outages of up to 12 hours at other periods.
details.energy_note: Five hours of power a day, as a normal year.

issues.title: Fishing inside a line drawn offshore
issues.category_name: Siege: water, power, fishing limits and the dual-use list
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living under the occupation, any gender
issues.summary: The fishing zone agreed at Oslo was 20 nautical miles. The enforced limit has been a fraction of that, which converts a fishing industry into a subsistence one.

details.aspect: The numbers
details.description: Fishermen were allowed less than a third of the area allocated under Oslo - six of 20 nautical miles. As of July 2014 Israel limited fishing to three nautical miles, barring access to the more fertile grounds. Oxfam notes the reduction from six to three prevented access to 85% of the waters agreed at Oslo.
details.energy_note: Eighty-five per cent of the sea, closed.

details.aspect: The fish are not in the permitted water
details.description: The sardine and larger pelagic grounds are further out. The permitted strip is over-fished, shallow and depleted, so effort rises while the catch falls.
details.money_note: Annual income difference for a fishing household.
details.energy_note: Fishing all day in the part with no fish.

details.aspect: Crossing the line is shot at
details.description: The limit is enforced by naval fire, arrest and boat confiscation. A navigational error is not a fine.
details.money_note: Value of a confiscated boat and gear.
details.energy_note: A wrong turn at sea is live fire.

details.aspect: It removes the cheapest protein from a food-insecure population
details.description: 57% of Gaza households were food insecure and about 80% were aid recipients. Restricting the fishery removes the one locally produced protein source that does not need a crossing permit.
details.energy_note: The one food nobody has to import, restricted.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - three miles of twenty
details.description: The Oslo Accords allocated 20 nautical miles. Fishermen were permitted six, and as of July 2014 Israel limited fishing to three - barring access to the more fertile grounds and, per Oxfam, preventing access to 85% of the waters agreed.
details.energy_note: Twenty miles on paper, three in the water.

issues.title: The list of things you may not import
issues.category_name: Siege: water, power, fishing limits and the dual-use list
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living under the occupation, any gender
issues.summary: The clearest documented absurdity in the whole file: for three years almost everything was banned unless specifically permitted, and the permitted list was never published.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - coriander, chocolate, toys and paper
details.description: From 2007 until the 2010 flotilla, Israel banned entry of countless goods including coriander, paper, toys and chocolate. Other than a narrow list of permitted items, which was never published, everything was banned. Coriander, chocolate, toys, certain fruits and notebooks were classified as luxuries, and entry depended on the will of unnamed Ministry of Defense officials.
details.energy_note: Coriander, classified as a security matter.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the calorie document
details.description: After a long legal campaign by Gisha, Israel's Ministry of Defense released documents titled 'Food Consumption in the Gaza Strip - Red Lines', containing the Health Ministry's estimate of the minimum calories an individual in Gaza needs. Israel said it was only a draft. An Israeli official acknowledged that some decisions behind product bans were irrational.
details.energy_note: A government calculating the minimum calories for a population.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the 2018 list
details.description: More than 1,000 basic commodities were again banned, including wedding dresses, cleaning sponges, baby bottles and nappies, along with fuel and gas.
details.energy_note: Wedding dresses and nappies, on a security list.

details.aspect: The dual-use list, and the fact that nobody can read it
details.description: The list comprises 56 items requiring special approval for the occupied territory generally, plus a Gaza-specific list. It was published only after a long legal battle, appeared in Hebrew first and later Arabic and English - and those translations then disappeared when COGAT relaunched its site.
details.energy_note: A published list that unpublished itself.

details.aspect: Gisha's lists are approximate because they have to be
details.description: Gisha's published lists are deduced from the approvals and denials traders receive, because Israeli authorities refuse to disclose the restrictions. The regulated parties reverse-engineer the regulation.
details.energy_note: Guessing the rules from the refusals.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the same chocolate, permitted or refused by who asked
details.description: Israel permitted some prohibited items - paper, biscuits, chocolate - if destined for international organisations, while denying private merchants' requests for the same goods.
details.energy_note: Identical box, different answer, depending on the letterhead.

details.aspect: In 2016 the procedure ceased to exist and the practice continued
details.description: COGAT confirmed in March 2016 that its 2010 procedure for bringing controlled goods into Gaza was no longer in effect - meaning it had no administrative directives detailing its own powers to prevent entry, while continuing to prevent it.
details.energy_note: Enforcing a rule that had been withdrawn.

details.aspect: Water and sewage pumps are on it, which closes the loop
details.description: A 2022 Oxfam report found the dual-use restrictions cover items such as water and sewage pumps, far exceeding international standards, with a listing process that 'appears arbitrary and is non-transparent'. The restriction causes the water crisis in SIE-001 and then blocks its repair.
details.energy_note: Banning the pump that would fix the water.

issues.title: Being blamed for the conditions the siege produced
issues.category_name: Siege: water, power, fishing limits and the dual-use list
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living under the occupation, any gender
issues.summary: Unemployment, aid dependency and a weak private sector are read abroad as evidence about Palestinians rather than as the measured outputs of a closure policy.

details.aspect: The figures that get quoted
details.description: 57% of households food insecure, about 80% aid recipients, 34.5% unemployment among those able and willing to work - one of the highest rates in the world.
